paras: The attempted lynching of Sam Sheeler took place at Otsego, Michigan, on August 19, 1895, when a crowd entered the jail, put a rope around the neck of Sheeler, a Black man accused of robbing and attempting to assault a woman, and dragged him from his cell. With the noose drawn tight he confessed and named companions, after which he was spared and returned to jail while posses hunted the other men. The story ran by wire across the country, and Virginia papers singled it out as a lynching attempt in the "staid law abiding North."

According to the wire reports, the Otsego area had suffered a run of robberies blamed on a gang, which one dispatch said had "terrorized this vicinity" for ten days. On the night of Sunday, August 18, a Black man broke into the house of a Mrs. Smith, forced her to give up jewelry, and attempted to assault her before her screams drove him away. A version printed in Michigan weeklies named her as Mrs. Geo. Smith and said the intruder held a revolver to her head and demanded her money and valuables.

The suspect was arrested at Plainwell on the morning of August 19, identified by Mrs. Smith, and held in the jail at Otsego. A crowd then gathered around the jail with a rope. The longer wire dispatch said the crowd "forced an entrance," while a shorter one said "a crowd of citizens" entered the jail "unresisted"; neither named any officer. Inside, the crowd put the rope around his neck and dragged him from his cell. As the noose drew tight he confessed, gave his name as Sam Sheeler of Fort Wayne, and named other Black men who he said could be found in a swamp near the town. The Belding Banner placed the confession at the moment "preparations were being made to swing him up" and said he named two companions, after which he was taken back to jail.

Posses then set out after the men he had named. By the wire account, the group was found two miles northwest of town and fired on its pursuers while trying to escape, and many shots were exchanged. Neighboring towns were notified, and the dispatch said the gang "will be killed if it does not surrender." The same report said there was still talk of lynching Sheeler and that he would probably be moved to Allegan for safekeeping.
The coverage does not report how the pursuit ended or whether Sheeler was tried, and no one in the crowd was reported arrested.

All of the coverage found appeared in white newspapers, carried by two different wire dispatches beginning on August 20. The longer dispatch, with the forced entry, the swamp and the gunfire, ran under headlines such as "Lost His Nerve," "Hung Until He Confessed" and "Must Surrender or Die." The shorter one, headed "Negro Nearly Lynched" or "Narrowly Escaped Lynching," ran in papers in Indiana, Delaware, Pennsylvania and Connecticut on August 20. It reached Wisconsin the next day and Michigan weeklies on August 23, and a condensed form appeared in the Bottineau Courant of North Dakota on August 31.

Every version treated the accusations as established, calling Sheeler "a colored thief" or "the brute," and the San Francisco Call headlined that he was "Compelled to Confess by the Aid of a Rope." The Michigan weekly version called him "the cowardly brute" and did not criticize the mob. In Virginia, the Richmond Dispatch headed the story "Lawlessness in Michigan," and the Richmond Times added "And This, Too, in the Staid Law Abiding North." Three days later the Clinch Valley News remarked that an attempt had been made to lynch a Black thief "in the staid and law abiding State of Michigan," describing the woman as white.

The two wire versions disagree on whether the crowd forced its way into the jail or met no resistance. Accounts of the confession also differ, naming "two or three" companions, "several other negroes" or two "pals." The surname appears as Sheeler in most papers but as Shelor in the Richmond papers, which also gave his expected destination as "Allenton" rather than Allegan.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sam Sheeler
bases: A crowd took Sheeler from his cell with a rope around his neck to hang him and released him only after he confessed, an attempted lynching in custody (A1, A10, A15).

A crowd acting without legal authority took Sheeler from jail with a rope over an accusation of robbery and attempted assault, but he confessed, was spared and was returned to jail, so no one was killed (A1, A8, A10); it was an attempted lynching.

Two different wire dispatches (A1/A3 and A2/A10) and a separately worded Michigan weekly account (A15) agree on the arrest, the rope, the dragging from the cell and the confession, though all come from the white press and none from a named local witness.
